title: Do I qualify for R&D tax credits if I’m a pre-revenue startup?
description: Pre-revenue U.S. startups can qualify for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41 if their work is qualified research.
summary: Pre-revenue U.S. startups can qualify for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41 if their work is qualified research. Because they have no income tax to offset, the key benefit is the qualified small business payroll tax election, letting companies with under $5 million in current-year gross receipts apply up to $500,000 annually against employer payroll taxes.

body.text: Pre-revenue U.S. startups can qualify for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41 if their work is qualified research. Because they have no income tax to offset, the key benefit is the qualified small business payroll tax election, letting companies with under $5 million in current-year gross receipts apply up to $500,000 annually against employer payroll taxes.
It is general information, not tax or legal advice.
Short answer

Yes, in many cases. A pre-revenue startup can earn the federal research credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) §41 if its work is qualified research. Because a company with no taxable income has no income tax to offset, the provision that matters most is the qualified small business (QSB) payroll tax election in IRC §41(h), which lets an eligible company apply part of its research credit against the employer’s payroll taxes. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, the annual election amount is up to $500,000 (the original $250,000, increased by $250,000).
First, the QSB gross receipts test is measured for the taxable year of the election, not over a five-year period.
Why pre-revenue status matters for the research credit
The credit and the income tax problem

The research credit under §41(a) is a credit against income tax and is part of the general business credit. Before 2016, it could be used only against income tax. A startup with no profit therefore earned credits it could not use right away; unused credits were carried to other years under the general business credit rules rather than paid out.
How the payroll election changed this

The Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015, Pub. L. No. 114-113, section 121(c), added IRC §41(h) and §3111(f), effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2015. Those sections let a qualified small business elect to apply part of its research credit against payroll tax instead of income tax. IRS Notice 2017-23 gives interim guidance on the election, including how the gross receipts tests apply.

The statute defines the amount that can move to payroll tax, called the payroll tax credit portion, as the least of three amounts (§41(h)(2)): the amount the company specifies in its election; the research credit for the year computed before the election; and, for a company other than a partnership or S corporation, the amount of the general business credit carryforward under §39 from that taxable year, determined before the election. For a pre-revenue C corporation with no income tax liability, the whole current-year research credit normally becomes a carryforward, so the third limit usually does not reduce the election, but it should be checked on the return.

Under §41(h)(1), the payroll tax credit portion is not treated as an income tax credit under §41(a), except for purposes of §280C. That exception matters for the research expense rules discussed later in this report.
Am I a qualified small business?
The two statutory tests
Under IRC §41(h)(3)(A), a corporation (including an S corporation) or a partnership is a qualified small business for a taxable year only if both of the following are true:

items: Its gross receipts for that taxable year are less than $5,000,000.
It had no gross receipts for any taxable year before the 5-taxable-year period ending with that taxable year.

body.text: An individual can also qualify by meeting the same tests, measured using the individual’s aggregate gross receipts from all trades or businesses.
The statute applies the $5,000,000 limit to the current taxable year alone.
Entities that cannot qualify

Under §41(h)(3)(B), an organization exempt from tax under §501 is not a qualified small business, whatever its gross receipts. A pre-revenue research venture organized as a nonprofit therefore cannot use the payroll election.
Controlled groups and related companies

Under §41(h)(5)(A), companies treated as a single taxpayer under the controlled group rules of §41(f)(1) are generally treated as one taxpayer for the QSB tests. Each member may make its own election, but the dollar limit is allocated among the members under the §41(f)(1) rules (§41(h)(5)(B)). A startup that is a subsidiary of, or under common control with, an older operating business should therefore test gross receipts and the receipts history at the group level.
The five-election limit

Under §41(h)(4)(B)(ii), no election is allowed for a taxable year if the company, or any person treated as a single taxpayer with it, made the election for 5 or more preceding taxable years. Together with the five-year receipts look-back, this limits the payroll election to a company’s early years.
What the tests mean in practice (analysis)

The second receipts test is a look-back on when a company first had receipts at all. A company that has been in business for a long time with occasional receipts can fail it even if its current receipts are small. Pre-revenue startups formed within the last few years are the companies most likely to pass both tests. Because the test counts gross receipts rather than revenue from customers, a founder should confirm with an adviser whether items such as interest income are gross receipts for this purpose before assuming the company has had none; Notice 2017-23 addresses the definition.
How the payroll tax offset works
Election amount and effective dates

cells: Beginning after December 31, 2015 and before January 1, 2023
IRC §41(h)(4)(B)(i), as amended by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, section 13902

body.text: The precise statutory wording is taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022. The IRS describes the change the same way on its page for the research credit against payroll tax, and the current Instructions for Form 6765 confirm the $500,000 maximum.
Which payroll taxes the credit offsets

That was the rule before the Inflation Reduction Act. Under §3111(f) as amended, and as the IRS describes it, starting in the first quarter of 2023 the credit first reduces the employer share of social security tax (up to $250,000 per quarter, in the IRS’s wording) and any remaining credit reduces the employer share of Medicare tax for the quarter. TIGTA’s April 2026 report on the credit describes the Medicare use as up to $250,000 of excess credit. Credit left after both reductions carries to the next quarter, and TIGTA notes that unused amounts can carry forward to later quarters until the credit is fully claimed.
Timing: when the cash benefit arrives

The election must specify the amount of credit to which it applies and must be made on or before the due date, including extensions, of the income tax return for the year (IRC §41(h)(4)(A)). For a partnership the relevant return is the §6031 return, and for an S corporation the §6037 return; for a partnership or S corporation the election is made at the entity level (§41(h)(4)(C)). The IRS’s internal processing guidance describes the election as made on Form 6765 filed with a timely filed (including extensions) original income tax return. The election and the elected amount go in Section D of Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, and the credit is then claimed on Form 8974, Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit for Increasing Research Activities, attached to the quarterly payroll return (Form 941, 943 or 944).

More precisely, the credit can first be claimed for the first calendar quarter that begins after the company files the income tax return that makes the election (§3111(f); IRS guidance; Form 8974 instructions). Once made, the election can be revoked only with the consent of the IRS (§41(h)(4)(A)).
Hypothetical worked example

Hypothetical. All figures are invented for illustration, and the elected amount is below every cap. A calendar-year startup passes both QSB tests, files its income tax return in March electing $120,000 of its research credit as a payroll tax credit, and so can begin claiming in the quarter starting April 1. Each quarter it owes $45,000 of employer social security tax and $10,500 of employer Medicare tax.

Check: $55,500 + $55,500 + $9,000 = $120,000. In Q2, $120,000 − $45,000 − $10,500 = $64,500; in Q3, $64,500 − $55,500 = $9,000. Social security is reduced first in each quarter, and only the amount remaining after that reduction is applied to Medicare, consistent with §3111(f) as amended.
The reported $780,000 example

The Asnani page does report this, but it does not name the company, give the tax years or show the calculation. (Analysis: because the annual election is capped at $500,000, a $780,000 total would have to span more than one tax year; the page does not say.) It should be read as an anecdote, not a benchmark.
Does the work qualify? The four-part test
QSB status only opens the payroll election. The underlying spending must still be qualified research under IRC §41(d) and the regulations.

cells: The research relates to a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality of a business component.
Uncertainty exists if the information available does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or its appropriate design.
The process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.
Substantially all of the activities are elements of a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result. “Substantially all” means 80 percent or more.

body.text: Following the 2025 legislation, §41(d)(1)(A) now ties qualified research to research with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under §174A. The first of the four tests in the table therefore depends on the cost first qualifying under §174A.

That matches §41(b)(3)(A): 65 percent of amounts paid or incurred to a person other than an employee for qualified research count as contract research expenses. The actual credit depends on the computation method the company uses on Form 6765.
Records needed to support a claim
What the regulation says

The governing regulation, Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d), requires a taxpayer claiming the credit to retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible, and points to the general record-retention rules in §1.6001-1. That regulation does not itself prescribe contemporaneous records or a particular format.
IRS oversight of the payroll credit

What the primary record does show is that the payroll credit is under review. TIGTA’s April 2026 report, titled “Controls for the Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit Were Updated, but Ineligible Taxpayers Continue to Receive the Credit,” describes IRS business rules that check Form 8974 fields and reports that ineligible taxpayers were still receiving the credit. The same report counts about 12,600 Forms 941 claiming $381 million of the credit for tax year 2024. A pre-revenue company should expect the QSB tests and the link between Form 6765 and Form 8974 to be checked.
Form 6765 Section G and qualified small businesses

The redesigned Form 6765 includes Section G, Business Component Information, which asks for qualified research expenses by business component. In IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), the IRS made Section G optional for all filers for tax year 2025 and announced that it will be mandatory for tax year 2026 and later, with optional reporting for qualified small businesses, as defined in §41(h)(3), that elect the payroll tax credit. The current Instructions for Form 6765 state that Section G is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to the guidelines in the Section G instructions. A pre-revenue company making the payroll election should confirm on the instructions for its year whether it falls within the QSB exception; even where Section G is optional, the underlying records must still meet §1.41-4(d).
Practical documentation (analysis)

Even without a contemporaneous-record mandate, records made while the work happens are usually easier to defend than accounts rebuilt later. These are reasonable ways to meet the “sufficiently usable form and detail” standard, and they map onto the four tests above. Organizing those records by business component also prepares a company for Section G if it later stops qualifying for the QSB exception.
Research expense amortization: updated rule

items: Under the version of §174 enacted by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 had to be amortized ratably over 5 years for domestic research.

Public Law 119-21 (July 4, 2025) added §174A, which allows a deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Section 174 now applies only to foreign research, which is still amortized over 15 years.

Rev. Proc. 2025-28, released August 28, 2025, lets eligible small business taxpayers apply §174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Eligibility turns on the §448(c) gross receipts test for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, and the taxpayer must not be a tax shelter; for a taxable year beginning in 2025, the inflation-adjusted threshold is $31,000,000.

Practitioner summaries of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 report that the retroactive election had to be made by July 6, 2026, or earlier if the period for claiming a refund closed first. That date has passed. A company that did not act should ask an adviser whether the accounting-method change route described in section 7.02(3)(c) of the revenue procedure is still available for its year.

Public Law 119-21 also amended §280C(c). As practitioners summarize it, a small business applying §174A retroactively must also apply the amended §280C(c) rules, and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 provides procedures to make a late reduced-credit election under §280C(c)(2) or to revoke an earlier one. Because §41(h)(1) treats the payroll tax credit portion as a §41(a) credit for §280C purposes, the payroll election does not take the credit outside these rules.

body.text: (Analysis: For domestic research in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, that pressure no longer applies in the same way. A pre-revenue company with losses rarely had income tax to pay even under amortization, though amortization reduced its net operating losses. The QSB payroll election remains the main route for a company with no income tax to offset.) One secondary summary (Ryan, Canadian edition) gives the §174A start date as taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025; the IRS revenue procedure says December 31, 2024, and controls.
Bottom line

A pre-revenue startup can qualify for the federal research credit and, if it meets both QSB tests for the year and is not tax-exempt, can elect to use up to $500,000 a year (for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022) against employer social security and then Medicare tax, for no more than five taxable years. The election is made in Section D of a timely filed Form 6765, can be revoked only with IRS consent, and the credit is claimed on Form 8974 starting with the first quarter after that return is filed. The research itself must pass the four-part test, the expenditures must be domestic research or experimental expenditures under §174A, and the company must keep records detailed enough to substantiate the claim, whether or not it completes Section G.
